# Synthesis from the International Drought experiment

We are going to replicate some of the regressions and figures from Smith et al. 2024. This PNAS paper was published with a link to Dryad, a popular data repository in ecology community run on FAIR principles. FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. 

### Q1 (1 point)
The full contents of the [Dryad repository](https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.3j9kd51rb) are in `data/`. From the README file, can  you tell what types of information are in each .csv? How would you assess this data repository in light of the FAIR criteria?

Yes, each csv has a description of the data stored within it. This dataset follows the FAIR principles, as it is easy to see where to find the data you might be interested in in the README, accessible online, uses common data files, and they have provided the code to reproduce all data analysis. 

### Q2 (1 point)
A single R script has been provided for this paper. Read through this file (running it is optional). Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of this code repository in light of your understanding of research compendia. 

The formatting of this script is helpful, as the associated statistics for each section/figure are included right before the figure in which they are used. In other words, all of the code associated with a specific question is grouped together. However, putting all of these sections in the same script makes it more difficult to find a specific analysis, rather than just run through everything. A more useful research compendia would include these analyses as separate scripts.

## Wrangling data

Since the goal of this exercise is to use linear regression and practice plotting, I have provided the code below for wrangling the data into a single dataframe:

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(patchwork)

# Figure 3 regression predictors
map <- read_csv("data/datappt_MAP2.csv") |> 
  select(-1, -X)
prior_ppt <- read_csv("data/datappt_pryr.csv") |> 
  select(-1)
map_cv <- read_csv("data/Dryad_submission_datappt_cv2.csv") |> 
  select(-1)
ai <- read_csv("data/datappt_ai3.csv") |> 
  select(-1)
sand <- read_csv("data/Dryad_submission_datapptsand2.csv") |> 
  select(-1)
graminoid <- read_csv("data/Dryad_submission_gram.ave.csv") |> 
  select(-1)
richness <- read_csv("data/Dryad_submission_datappt_rich2.csv") |> 
  select(-1)

# Figure 4 drought severity
drought_severity <- read_csv("data/data.Drtsite.csv") |> 
  select(-1)

# Create full dataset from above
data_all <- read_csv("data/data.hab.csv") |> 
  select(-1) |> 
  rename(habitat_type = habitat.type) |> 
  left_join(map) |> 
  relocate(precip, .after = Sig) |> 
  left_join(prior_ppt |> 
              select(site_code, drtpct_map730)) |> 
  left_join(map_cv |> 
              select(site_code, cv_ppt_inter)) |> 
  left_join(ai |> 
              select(site_code, logAI)) |> 
  left_join(sand|> 
              select(site_code, sand_mean)) |> 
  left_join(graminoid |> 
              select(site_code, prop.ave)) |> 
  left_join(richness |> 
              select(site_code, average.richness)) |> 
  left_join(drought_severity|> 
              select(site_code, mean_drt2)) |> 
  rename(DR = mean_DS3, # Drought response
         MAP = precip,
         prev_precip = drtpct_map730,
         MAP_cv = cv_ppt_inter,
         lnAridity = logAI,
         gram_prop = prop.ave,
         rich_mean = average.richness,
         DS = mean_drt2) # Drought severity
```

## Univariate drivers of drought response (Fig. 3)

### Q3 (1 point)
From the published R code, it appears that Fig. 3 was made in separate pieces. Recreate the figure to the best of your ability with a single code chunk, using `facet_wrap()`. 
 
```{r}
theme_set(theme_classic())

make_panels <- function(var, regression, xlab, panel_letter) {
  regression_color = NA
  regression_fill = NA
  
  if (regression) {
    regression_color = 'black'
    regression_fill = 'grey50'
  }
  
  panel <- data_all |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = var, y = DR)) +
    annotate("text", x = min(var, na.rm = TRUE), y = 0.5, label = panel_letter, size = 10) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5) +
    geom_point(aes(color = habitat_type, shape = Eco.Extr), size = 3) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("springgreen4", "sienna")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 1, 17, 2)) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "Drought Response") +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.title = element_text(size = 15),
          axis.text = element_text(size = 13)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = regression_color, fill = regression_fill) 
  
  
  panel
}

panel_a <- make_panels(data_all$MAP, TRUE, 'MAP (mm)', 'A')
panel_b <- make_panels(data_all$prev_precip, FALSE, 'Previous Precipitation (mm)', 'B')
panel_c <- make_panels(data_all$MAP_cv, FALSE, 'CV of MAP (%)', 'C')
panel_d <- make_panels(data_all$lnAridity, TRUE, 'ln(Aridity Index)', 'D')
panel_e <- make_panels(data_all$sand_mean, FALSE, 'Sand in Soil (%)', 'E')
panel_f <- make_panels(data_all$gram_prop, FALSE, 'Proportion of Graminoids', 'F')
panel_g <- make_panels(data_all$rich_mean, TRUE, 'Average Richness', 'G')

plot_grid(panel_a, panel_b, panel_c, panel_d, panel_e, panel_f, panel_g)

```

## Testing the Inverse Texture hypothesis
See Prof. Guo's slides on the inverse texture hypothesis. Under this hypothesis, there should be a significant interaction term between which two variables?

There should be a significant interaction term between MAP and productivity. This interaction is modulated by % sand in the soil.

### Q4 (1 point)
Conduct a multiple regression to test the inverse texture hypothesis. Is there statistical support for this hypothesis? Write your answer as a results sentence, including appropriate statistics. 

```{r}
m1 <- lm(DR ~ MAP + sand_mean, data = data_all)
summary(m1)
anova(m1)
```

These data show no relationship between MAP and drought response (productivity) (F = 1.885, df = 2, 93, p = 0.8436). 

### Q5 (1 point)
Compare your result above to the supplemental Table S7. Try using 'lme4' and lmer() to replicate the results of Table S7. Were you successful? If not, what is the limiting factor?


```{r}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

m2 <- lmer(DR ~ MAP + sand_mean + MAP * sand_mean + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m2)
```

We were successful! When we first tried this, we followed what the caption said, which was to treat site as the random effect. However, since we only have one observation per site, there is not enough statistical power to treat site as the random effect. So, we tried treating habitat type as the random effect instead, and found that this output matched the table from the supplement.

## Importance of drought severity (Fig. 4)

### Q6 (1 point)
Replicate the simple linear regression in Fig. 4. 

```{r}
  
data_some <- data_all |> 
  group_by(Extreme) |> 
  summarize(mean_DS = mean(DS), mean_DR = mean(DR))

data_all |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = DS, y = DR)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = -.7), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5, color = 'red') +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = -1.3), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5, color = 'red') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = habitat_type, shape = Eco.Extr), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("springgreen4", "sienna")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(15, 16, 1, 0, 17, 2)) +
  labs(x = 'Drought Severity', y = "Drought Response") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = 'black', fill = 'grey50') +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.title = element_text(size = 15),
          axis.text = element_text(size = 13)) + 
  geom_point(data = data_some, aes(x = mean_DR, y = mean_DS, shape = Extreme), color = 'orange', size = 7) + 
  annotate("text", x = .15, y = -.8, label = '-50%', size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = .15, y = -1.4, label = '-75%', size = 5)
  
```

How much variation in drought response is explained by drought severity? How does this compare to the coefficient of determination (R^2) of the predictors in Fig. 3?

```{r}
m2 <- lm(DR ~ DS + Extreme, data = data_all)
summary(m2)
```

Based on our R^2 of 0.06981, only around 7% of the variation in drought response is explained by drought severity. This is slightly better than the R^2 values of the predictors in figure 3, many of which are insignificant. Our metric is close to the R^2 values of the best predictors from figure 3, which have R^2 values of around 0.05.

### Q7 (1 point)
It can be unsatisfying to run numerous simple linear regressions. We also increase the risk of Type I error, meaning that due to the large number of hypothesis tests, we are more likely to see a false positive even if that relationship isn't truly significant. 

In the supplemental Table S8, Smith et al. 2024 show the output of a multiple regression. Replicate this below to the best of your ability. 

```{r}
m2 <- lmer(DR ~ DS + MAP + prev_precip + MAP_cv + sand_mean + gram_prop + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m2)
```

How much more variation in drought response is predicted by this ensemble of predictor variables? 

Based on the R^2 of 0.1, this ensemble model accounts for around twice as much variation in drought response as the best individual predictors from figure 3 (MAP: R^2 of 0.05).

Which variable does the heavy lifting, and how does this compare to the results of the simple linear regression?

The drought severity index does the heavy lifting, accounting for the most variance of any predictor. Drought severity is also the best predictor in the simple linear regression, again accounting for more variance than the other predictor.


### Q8 (1 point)
One common consideration in multiple regression is multicollinearity of the predictor variable. Look up the documentation for `pairs()` and use it on all of the predictor columns in `data_all`. Which predictors are strongly correlated? What does this suggest about their usage in a multiple regression model?

```{r}
pairs(data_all |> select(DR, MAP, prev_precip, MAP_cv, lnAridity, sand_mean, gram_prop, rich_mean, DS))
```

MAP and lnAridity are the predictor variables with the strongest linear correlation. This means that they would have the same explanatory power in a model. This could falsely improve model performance, so one of these two variables should likely be removed from a multiple linear regression.


### Q9 (2 points)
When there are multiple possible predictor variables to choose from, we can use model selection methods to identify the 'best' overall model. 'Best' cannot be only based on high R^2 values, as that would promote overfitting such that conclusions are unlikely to be applicable to a new context. Therefore, 'best' is often determined by the tradeoff between high model fit and low model complexity. Often, the target statistic to minimize is an information criterion, which consists of two components:

$IC = likelihood - penalty$ 

where the likelihood is a metric of model fit and the penalty is a metric of model complexity. The adjusted $R^2$ in the `lm()` output is one such IC. Another common information criterion you may encounter is the AIC, or Akaike Information Criterion:

$AIC = -2ln(L) + 2k$

where ln(L) is the log-likelihood and k is the number of parameters in the model. A model with a smaller AIC value is deemed 'better' at predicting new data than a model with a larger AIC value, given the same response variable being modeled. 

Try a backward selection approach (starting with the model from Q7) and sequentially reduce number of predictors (removing the highest p-value) until the model's AIC stops decreasing. How does this model compare to the multiple regression model used by Smith et al. (2024)?

Note that model comparison can only be done on the same response data, so you may have reduce your dataset in advance. 

```{r}
# model from Q7
m <- lmer(DR ~ DS + MAP + prev_precip + MAP_cv + sand_mean + gram_prop + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m)
AIC(m)

# removing MAP
m <- lmer(DR ~ DS + prev_precip + MAP_cv + sand_mean + gram_prop + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m)
AIC(m)

# removing sand_mean
m <- lmer(DR ~ DS + prev_precip + MAP_cv + gram_prop + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m)
AIC(m)

# removing gram_prop
m <- lmer(DR ~ DS + prev_precip + MAP_cv + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m)
AIC(m)
# this caused an increase in AIC, so our previous model is better

# optimized model
m <- lmer(DR ~ DS + prev_precip + MAP_cv + gram_prop + (1|habitat_type), data = data_all)
summary(m)
AIC(m)
```

Based on table S11, where a series of models are compared, Smith et al. found that MAP and previous year precipitation were the least efficient predictor variables based on AIC. They included variables such as lnAridity and richness than our model did not include. Of the shared variables, both our model and Smith et al.'s show that drought severity is the most efficient predictor variable based on AIC. Our model optimization also found that MAP was an inefficient predictor, but did still include previous year precipitation. 

They explicitly report performing a multiple linear regression in the paper, but we found that no data or further information appears on this either in the paper or in the supplemental data.
